blocks.text: Hydrocarbons are the class of organic compounds that consist of carbon and hydrogen only. They are abundant in petroleum and natural gas and are widely used as domestic and industrial fuels, and they have many synthetic applications: unsaturated hydrocarbons, especially alkenes, are the starting materials for many industrial products, and most medicines, plastics, perfumes and polymers have their origins in hydrocarbons. Hydrocarbons are broadly divided into two classes, aliphatic and aromatic.

blocks.title: Aliphatic hydrocarbons
blocks.text: Compounds that are not aromatic are called aliphatic. Aliphatic compounds may be open chain or cyclic, and saturated or unsaturated; if they contain only carbon and hydrogen they are aliphatic hydrocarbons. Alkanes are acyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons, cycloalkanes are cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons, and alkenes and alkynes are acyclic, unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons (Figure 11.1: methane, ethane, ethene, ethyne, cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, cyclohexane).

blocks.title: Aromatic hydrocarbons
blocks.text: Aromatic hydrocarbons are a special class of cyclic hydrocarbons with a high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, based on benzene (C6H6) or resembling compounds. Benzene is the basic aromatic compound; toluene and phenol are its derivatives (Figure 11.2: benzene, methylbenzene, ethylbenzene). The term aromatic comes from the Greek 'aroma', fragrant, for the characteristic odour of these compounds.

blocks.long_description: Aliphatic hydrocarbons are everything that is not aromatic: open chains such as the alkanes methane and ethane, the alkene ethene and the alkyne ethyne, and rings such as cyclopropane to cyclohexane, each corner of a ring standing for a CH2 group. Aromatic hydrocarbons are built on the benzene ring, drawn as a hexagon with a circle for its delocalised electrons, with toluene and ethylbenzene as substituted examples. The alkanes form a homologous series with the general formula CnH2n+2, each member one CH2 longer than the last, and removing one hydrogen from an alkane gives an alkyl group named with the ending -yl.

blocks.prompt: Differentiate aliphatic from aromatic hydrocarbons, and classify cyclohexane, ethyne and toluene (exercise Q.2b).
blocks.explanation: Aliphatic hydrocarbons are those not based on the benzene ring: open-chain or cyclic, saturated or unsaturated, such as cyclohexane (a cyclic saturated aliphatic hydrocarbon) and ethyne (an acyclic unsaturated one). Aromatic hydrocarbons contain the benzene ring, with a high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, such as toluene (methylbenzene).

items: Hydrocarbons: C and H only; fuels from petroleum and natural gas; alkenes are industrial starting materials.
Aliphatic = not aromatic (alkanes acyclic, cycloalkanes cyclic, alkenes and alkynes unsaturated). Aromatic = benzene-based rings with a high C : H ratio (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene).
